title: Effects of Resistance Training on Glycemic Control and Cardiovascular Risk Factors in Type 2 Diabetes

mappings.3862587: This is a randomized controlled trial. Participants with Type 2 Diabetes will be randomly assigned to either a resistance training group or a control group (no exercise intervention). The resistance training group will complete a supervised 12-week progressive resistance training program 3 days per week. The control group will be asked to maintain their current level of physical activity and will be offered the resistance training program upon completion of the study. Assessments will be conducted at baseline (week 0) and post-intervention (week 12).
mappings.3862588: Primary outcomes include glycemic control as measured by HbA1c and fasting blood glucose. Secondary outcomes include cardiovascular risk factors (resting blood pressure, lipid profile including total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides), body composition (body mass, BMI, waist circumference, body fat percentage via DEXA), and muscular strength (1-RM for leg press and chest press).
mappings.3862589: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) affects approximately 37.3 million Americans and is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Chronic hyperglycemia in T2DM is associated with increased risk for cardiovascular disease, neuropathy, nephropathy, and retinopathy. While aerobic exercise has been widely studied as a therapeutic intervention for T2DM, resistance training has received comparatively less attention despite emerging evidence that it may independently improve glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors. Resistance training has been shown to improve insulin sensitivity by increasing skeletal muscle glucose uptake and GLUT-4 transporter activity. Furthermore, resistance training increases lean body mass, which may contribute to improved basal metabolic rate and long-term glycemic management. Several meta-analyses have demonstrated that resistance training can reduce HbA1c by 0.3-0.6%, which is clinically meaningful. However, many of these studies have methodological limitations including small sample sizes, short intervention durations, and inadequate control of confounding variables such as dietary intake and medication changes. Additional research using rigorous randomized controlled trial designs is needed to further elucidate the effects of resistance training on glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors in individuals with T2DM. This study aims to address these gaps by implementing a well-controlled 12-week progressive resistance training intervention and assessing comprehensive metabolic and cardiovascular outcomes.
mappings.3862593: The Human Performance Laboratory (HPL) in the Department of Kinesiology, Bailey Building, TCU campus.
mappings.3862644: Participants must meet the following inclusion criteria: (1) physician-diagnosed Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus for at least 6 months; (2) age 30-65 years; (3) HbA1c between 6.5% and 10.0%; (4) BMI between 25 and 40 kg/m2; (5) not currently participating in a structured resistance training program (defined as less than 2 sessions per week for the past 3 months); (6) able to provide written informed consent; (7) physician clearance to participate in a resistance training program.
mappings.3862645: Participants will be excluded if they meet any of the following criteria: (1) Type 1 Diabetes or gestational diabetes; (2) insulin pump use; (3) uncontrolled hypertension (resting blood pressure >160/100 mmHg); (4) history of cardiovascular event (myocardial infarction, stroke) within the past 12 months; (5) musculoskeletal condition or injury that would preclude safe participation in resistance training; (6) current pregnancy or planning to become pregnant during the study period; (7) changes in diabetes medication type or dosage within the past 3 months; (8) diagnosed peripheral neuropathy that limits exercise capacity; (9) proliferative retinopathy; (10) severe autonomic neuropathy.
mappings.3862663: Participants will be recruited from the greater Fort Worth community through multiple methods: (1) flyers posted at local endocrinology and primary care clinics (with clinic approval via letters of support); (2) flyers posted on the TCU campus; (3) social media advertisements through the TCU Kinesiology Department social media accounts; (4) word of mouth referrals from physicians and current participants. Recruitment materials will include basic study information, eligibility criteria, and contact information for the research team. Interested individuals will be directed to contact the research team by phone or email for initial eligibility screening.
mappings.3862673: 1. Potential participants who contact the research team will first undergo a brief telephone screening to determine preliminary eligibility based on self-reported information (age, diabetes type and duration, current exercise habits, and general health history). Those who appear eligible will be invited to an in-person screening visit at the Human Performance Laboratory. 2. At the screening visit, the research team will verify eligibility by reviewing the participant's physician clearance form, confirming diabetes diagnosis via medical documentation, and measuring resting blood pressure, height, weight, and HbA1c via point-of-care testing. 3. Both identifiable (name, phone number, email) and non-identifiable (age, exercise history) information will be collected during the screening process. 4. The telephone screening will take approximately 10-15 minutes. The in-person screening visit will take approximately 45-60 minutes.
mappings.3862674: 1. Data collected during screening for individuals who are not eligible or who choose not to participate will be destroyed. Specifically, their contact information and screening forms will be shredded (paper documents) or permanently deleted (electronic files) within 30 days of the determination of ineligibility or the decision not to participate. 2. Screening data for individuals who enroll in the study will be retained as part of the study records and stored with other study data in the PI's locked office and on the password-protected TCU OneDrive.
mappings.3862689: Informed consent will be obtained by the PI or a trained member of the research team during the in-person screening visit, prior to any study procedures. The consent process will take place in a private room within the Human Performance Laboratory. The research team member obtaining consent will explain the study purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, and the participant's right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Participants will be given a copy of the consent form to read at their own pace and will have the opportunity to ask questions. If the participant agrees to participate, they will sign and date two copies of the consent form; one copy will be retained by the research team and one copy will be given to the participant for their records. Participants will be informed that their participation is voluntary and that they may withdraw at any time without any impact on their medical care.
mappings.3862692: Participants may withdraw from the study at any time without penalty or loss of benefits to which they are otherwise entitled. If a participant wishes to withdraw, they should notify the PI or a member of the research team. Data collected up to the point of withdrawal will be retained and included in analyses unless the participant specifically requests that their data be destroyed. If a participant experiences a change in health status that makes continued participation unsafe (e.g., uncontrolled blood pressure, new cardiovascular event, injury), the PI will discontinue the participant from the study and refer them back to their physician. The PI also reserves the right to discontinue a participant's involvement if it is in the best interest of the participant's safety.
mappings.3862869:
All study procedures will be conducted at the Human Performance Laboratory (HPL) in the Bailey Building on the TCU campus.

Baseline Assessment (Week 0): After providing informed consent and completing the screening visit, eligible participants will complete baseline assessments including: (1) fasting blood draw for HbA1c, fasting glucose, and lipid panel (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides) performed by a certified phlebotomist; (2) body composition assessment via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan; (3) anthropometric measurements (height, weight, BMI, waist circumference); (4) resting blood pressure measured after 5 minutes of seated rest using an automated oscillometric device (average of 3 readings); (5) muscular strength assessment via one-repetition maximum (1-RM) testing for leg press and chest press. 1-RM testing will follow the NSCA guidelines with appropriate warm-up sets and rest periods between attempts.

Resistance Training Intervention (Weeks 1-12): Participants randomized to the resistance training group will complete supervised resistance training sessions 3 days per week (typically Monday, Wednesday, Friday) for 12 weeks at the HPL. Each session will last approximately 60 minutes and include a 5-minute warm-up, 45-50 minutes of resistance exercises, and a 5-minute cool-down. The program will include 8 exercises targeting major muscle groups: leg press, leg curl, leg extension, chest press, lat pulldown, seated row, shoulder press, and bicep curl. The program will be progressive: Weeks 1-4: 2 sets of 12-15 repetitions at 60-65% 1-RM; Weeks 5-8: 3 sets of 10-12 repetitions at 65-75% 1-RM; Weeks 9-12: 3 sets of 8-10 repetitions at 75-85% 1-RM. Rest periods between sets will be 60-90 seconds. All sessions will be supervised by trained research personnel who will ensure proper form and technique, monitor for adverse events, and record training loads.

Control Group (Weeks 1-12): Participants in the control group will be asked to maintain their current level of physical activity and dietary habits for the 12-week study period. Control group participants will receive weekly check-in phone calls to monitor health status and physical activity levels. They will be offered the resistance training program at the conclusion of the study.

Post-Intervention Assessment (Week 12): All participants will repeat the same battery of assessments completed at baseline: fasting blood draw, DEXA scan, anthropometric measurements, resting blood pressure, and 1-RM testing.

Participants in both groups will be asked to maintain a 3-day food diary at baseline and during week 12 to monitor dietary intake. They will also be asked to report any changes in diabetes medication throughout the study period.
mappings.3862824: Participants will be randomly assigned to either the resistance training group or the control group using a computer-generated random number sequence created by a research team member not involved in data collection. Randomization will occur after the baseline assessment is completed. The allocation sequence will be concealed in sequentially numbered, sealed opaque envelopes. The PI will open the envelope and inform the participant of their group assignment.
mappings.3862828: The control group will not receive the resistance training intervention during the 12-week study period. They will be asked to maintain their current level of physical activity. The rationale for using a no-exercise control group is to isolate the effects of the resistance training intervention on the study outcomes. To enhance retention and reduce the ethical concern of withholding a potentially beneficial intervention, control group participants will be offered the full 12-week resistance training program at the conclusion of the study.
mappings.3862820: 1. Fasting venous blood samples (approximately 10 mL per draw) will be collected from an antecubital vein by a certified phlebotomist at baseline and post-intervention. Participants will be instructed to fast for at least 8 hours and to avoid strenuous exercise for 24 hours prior to the blood draw. Blood samples will be collected into appropriate vacutainer tubes (EDTA for HbA1c, SST for glucose and lipids). 2. Blood samples will be processed (centrifuged, aliquoted) within 30 minutes of collection at the HPL and transported in a cooler with ice packs to the designated laboratory for analysis. Samples will be stored temporarily at -80 degrees Celsius if not analyzed immediately. 3. Samples will be stored for the duration of the analysis period, no longer than 6 months after the final participant completes the study. 4. Samples will be used only for the analyses described in this protocol. 5. All blood sample processing and analysis will be conducted on the TCU campus in the Department of Kinesiology laboratory. The laboratory is not CLIA certified as this is a research laboratory; results will not be used for clinical diagnosis.
mappings.3862811: Blood samples will be collected using standard venipuncture technique by a certified phlebotomist. Universal precautions will be followed at all times during blood collection, processing, and disposal. Sharps will be disposed of in designated sharps containers. Blood-contaminated materials will be disposed of in biohazard bags. The phlebotomist and all research personnel handling blood samples will have current bloodborne pathogen training. Blood collection supplies (needles, vacutainers, alcohol swabs, gauze, bandages) will be stored in the HPL and checked for expiration dates regularly.
mappings.3863061: There will be no direct costs to participants for any study procedures. Parking will be available at no cost on the TCU campus. Participants will be responsible for their own transportation to and from the study site.
mappings.3863065: Participants will be compensated for their time and effort. Participants in both groups will receive $25 for completing each assessment visit (baseline and post-intervention) for a total of $50. In addition, participants in the resistance training group will receive $5 per completed training session (maximum of 36 sessions over 12 weeks) for a total possible training compensation of $180. Therefore, the maximum total compensation for the resistance training group is $230 and for the control group is $50. Compensation will be provided in the form of Visa gift cards distributed at the post-intervention assessment visit. Participants who withdraw from the study will receive prorated compensation for completed activities ($25 per completed assessment visit and $5 per completed training session).
mappings.3863068:
Potential risks include:

1. Musculoskeletal injury: Resistance training carries a risk of muscle strains, joint sprains, and other musculoskeletal injuries. To minimize this risk, all training sessions will be supervised by trained research personnel, proper warm-up will precede all sessions, proper exercise form and technique will be demonstrated and monitored, and the progressive overload protocol allows for gradual adaptation. Participants will be instructed to stop exercise immediately and notify the supervisor if they experience pain.

2. Cardiovascular event: There is a small risk of a cardiovascular event (e.g., abnormal blood pressure response) during exercise. To minimize this risk, participants must obtain physician clearance prior to enrollment. Blood pressure will be monitored before each training session. Participants with uncontrolled hypertension will be excluded. Research personnel will be trained in CPR and emergency procedures, and an AED will be available in the HPL.

3. Hypoglycemia: Participants with T2DM may experience exercise-induced hypoglycemia. To minimize this risk, participants will be advised to check blood glucose before each session. If blood glucose is below 100 mg/dL, participants will be asked to consume a snack before training. If blood glucose is above 300 mg/dL, the session will be postponed. Glucose tablets and juice will be available at each session. Research personnel will be trained to recognize and respond to signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia.

4. Venipuncture risks: Blood draws carry minor risks including bruising, bleeding, infection, and lightheadedness. These risks will be minimized by using a certified phlebotomist and standard aseptic technique. Participants will be seated during blood draws.

5. DEXA scan: The DEXA scan exposes participants to a very low dose of radiation (approximately 1-5 microSieverts per scan), which is well below the annual occupational exposure limit and comparable to the natural background radiation received in a few hours. The risk from this exposure is negligible.

6. Breach of confidentiality: There is a minimal risk that participant information could be inadvertently disclosed. To minimize this risk, data will be de-identified and stored securely as described in the data management plan.

7. Psychological risks: There is a minimal risk of frustration or anxiety related to exercise testing, blood draws, or body composition assessment. Participants will be informed that they can stop any procedure at any time and can withdraw from the study without penalty.
mappings.3863069: There may be direct benefits to participants in the resistance training group, including improved glycemic control, improved cardiovascular risk profile, increased muscular strength, and improved body composition. Control group participants may benefit from the resistance training program offered at the end of the study. All participants may benefit from learning about their health status through the assessments performed at baseline and post-intervention. There is no guarantee that any participant will receive direct benefit from participation. The potential benefits to society include contributing to the scientific understanding of the effects of resistance training on glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors in individuals with Type 2 Diabetes, which may inform clinical exercise recommendations for this population.
mappings.3863071: All study data will be de-identified using a unique participant ID number. A master linking file connecting participant names to ID numbers will be stored in a separate password-protected file on the PI's TCU OneDrive account, accessible only to the PI. All paper documents (consent forms, screening forms, data collection sheets) will be stored in a locked filing cabinet in the PI's locked office in the Bailey Building. All electronic data will be stored on the PI's password-protected TCU OneDrive account. Only members of the research team will have access to the de-identified data. Blood samples will be labeled with participant ID numbers only and stored in the locked laboratory at -80 degrees Celsius. Research activities (assessments and training sessions) will be conducted in the HPL, which is a private space within the Bailey Building, ensuring participant privacy during study procedures. DEXA scans will be conducted in a private room with only the participant and same-sex research team member present. The 3-day food diaries will be collected and stored with other paper documents in the locked filing cabinet. All data will be retained for a minimum of 3 years following the completion of the study, after which paper documents will be shredded and electronic files will be permanently deleted.
mappings.3863075: Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations) will be calculated for all outcome variables at baseline and post-intervention for both groups. Independent samples t-tests will be used to compare baseline characteristics between groups to verify successful randomization. The primary analysis will use a 2 (group: resistance training vs. control) x 2 (time: baseline vs. post-intervention) mixed-model analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each outcome variable. The between-subjects factor will be group and the within-subjects factor will be time. The primary outcome of interest will be the group x time interaction effect. If significant interaction effects are found, post-hoc pairwise comparisons will be conducted using Bonferroni correction. Effect sizes (Cohen's d) will be calculated for all significant findings. An intent-to-treat analysis approach will be used, with last observation carried forward for missing data. Statistical significance will be set at p < 0.05. All analyses will be conducted using SPSS (version 29). A power analysis was conducted a priori using G*Power software, indicating that a sample of 34 participants (17 per group) is needed to detect a medium effect size (f = 0.25) with 80% power at an alpha level of 0.05 for the group x time interaction effect. To account for an estimated 15% attrition rate, we will aim to enroll 40 participants (20 per group).
mappings.3863076: The PI will serve as the data safety monitor for this study. The PI will review all adverse events and will be responsible for determining whether the study should be modified or terminated based on safety concerns. Adverse events will be documented on an adverse event form and reported to the TCU IRB in accordance with IRB policies. The PI will review study data on an ongoing basis to monitor for any unexpected patterns or safety signals. If a serious adverse event occurs that is related to the study procedures, the PI will immediately suspend the study and report to the IRB within 24 hours.
